title: The machine learning pipeline
hook: Data, training, testing, running it live, and watching it. Predict returns from a table.
inPlainWords: Most business AI is still rows and columns. The pipeline is the same every time: collect data, clean it, hold some back as an exam, train, test, run it live, and keep watching.

useCase.title: Predict which orders will be returned
useCase.story: ShopEase has 30,000 past orders in a table: item, size, price, customer history, and whether it was returned. The warehouse wants a warning flag on risky orders.

approaches.name: Gut-feel rules
approaches.greatWhen: Day one, with no data cleanup.
approaches.avoidWhen: Patterns are subtle or change with the season.
approaches.example: Shoes above $100 that run small get flagged.

approaches.name: Classic ML on the table
approaches.what: Tree-based models learn which columns matter from past rows.
approaches.greatWhen: Rows-and-columns business data, which is the usual case.
approaches.avoidWhen: The data is images, audio or long text.
approaches.example: It learns that ordering three sizes of the same shoe often means a return.

approaches.name: AutoML tool
approaches.what: A tool tries many models for you and ranks them.
approaches.greatWhen: You want a fast first baseline with a small team.
approaches.avoidWhen: You must explain and control every step.
approaches.example: Upload the table and get ranked models within the hour.

approaches.name: Deep learning
approaches.what: A neural network learns from the raw table.
approaches.greatWhen: Very large data, images or text.
approaches.avoidWhen: Small tables, where it is usually no better and much harder to explain.
approaches.example: Forcing a neural network onto 30,000 rows.

approaches.name: Ask a language model per row
approaches.what: Send each order to a language model and ask "will it be returned?"
approaches.greatWhen: Almost never for this kind of task.
approaches.avoidWhen: Number-heavy tables. It is slow, costly, and its confidence is not backed by your data.
approaches.example: It says "probably not" and cannot show any evidence.

challenge.question: You have 30,000 rows in a spreadsheet and a yes/no answer for each. What is the best tool?

options.why: Built for rows and columns. Quick, cheap and explainable.
Not enough data to justify it, and it is harder to explain.

options.text: Ask a language model about each order
options.why: Slow, costly, and it has never seen your return patterns.
A good baseline to beat, but it will miss subtle patterns.

bestCase.title: Classic ML, tested on orders it has never seen
bestCase.example: The model flags 1 in 5 orders as risky, and 6 in 10 of the flagged orders really come back. The team adds a size guide to those product pages and returns fall.

worstCase.title: Peeking at the answer, and never checking again
worstCase.example: You leave in the column "return reason", which only exists after a return. The model scores 99% in testing and is useless live. Six months later new-season products arrive and nobody notices accuracy fading.

steps.label: Past orders table
steps.goes: 30,000 rows, each with the known answer: returned or not.

steps.label: Clean and choose columns
steps.goes: Fix blanks and drop any column you would not know at order time.
steps.goesWrong: "Return reason" is left in. It is only known after the return.

steps.label: Split: practice and exam
steps.goes: 80% is used for learning. 20% is hidden as an exam.

steps.label: Train the model
steps.goes: The model finds which patterns predict returns.

steps.label: Sit the exam
steps.goes: Check it works on orders it has never seen.

steps.label: Run it live
steps.goes: A new order goes in, a risk flag comes out, in milliseconds.

steps.label: Watch and retrain
steps.goes: Check accuracy monthly and retrain each season.

takeaway: Test on data the model has never seen, and keep watching it after launch. Both are where projects quietly fail.
